sources.news_title: Another ‘Drug Kingpin’ Captured
sources.text:
The Mexico government on Friday captured alleged drug kingpin Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores and two other alleged high-level members of his organization.
As reported at CBS News, the United States government was involved in the pursuit and capture of Meza-Flores. This involvement included the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) including Meza-Fores on its Ten Most Wanted list, the US obtaining an indictment of him, the US offering an up to five million dollars reward for information leading directly to his arrest or conviction, and the US providing intelligence that the Mexico government has said helped bring about his capture.
Drug war boosters in America will claim that the capture of Meza-Flores is a victory against the threat of drugs and for the safety of Americans. However, the capture of this man, like the capture and killing of others before him, will do nothing to advance those goals. In fact, it will be counterproductive to advancing those goals while playing a part in the US drug war’s ongoing attack on the freedom of Americans. For analysis of why this is the case, take a look at my November of 2025 article “The DOJ is Prosecuting a Drug Kingpin, Blah, Blah, Blah.” The article concerns the prosecution in the US, then, of another alleged drug kingpin — Zhi Dong Zhang — upon Mexico extraditing him to the US. Here we are a year later with the same sorry story repeating.

sources.news_title: Mexico Confirms Four Soldiers, Seven Gunmen Killed During Arrest of Sinaloa Kingpin
sources.text:
Despite an intense hours-long shootout involving dozens of armored trucks, .50 caliber weapons, and explosives, that brought the state of Sinaloa to a standstill, Mexico’s government revealed that only four soldiers and seven gunmen died.
The low number of casualties highlights the effectiveness of Mexican troops who worked with U.S. intelligence to track down and arrest one of the most powerful drug lords in Mexico. As Breitbart Texas reported, on Friday night, Mexico’s military raided a series of properties in the city of Guasave, the stronghold of Isidro “Chapo Isidro” Meza Flores, the leader of the Beltran Leyva Cartel.
Information provided to Breitbart Texas by Mexico’s Security Cabinet revealed that the military set up a perimeter to prevent escapes and to block cartel reinforcements from arriving as a core group of special forces soldiers moved in to arrest El Chapo Isidro.
During his more than 15-year reign as head of the Beltran Leyva Cartel, Meza set himself apart by largely avoiding unnecessary conflict, but he had an army of highly trained paramilitary troops feared by other cartels. In recent months, Meza’s troops had been highly effective in fighting off incursions from Cartel Jalisco New Generation, as well as Los Chapitos. Those incursions led El Chapo Isidro to join forces with Los Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel after months of trying to avoid picking sides in the fierce turf war between Los Chapitos and Los Mayos.
Meza has long been a target of the U.S. government, which had offered a large reward for his capture. His arrest in Mexico follows an extradition warrant, since he is wanted in the United States on terrorism and drug charges. The arrest was highly praised by the U.S. government, which has been pressuring Mexico to take a more active role in fighting drug cartels.
His arrest was also met with congratulations from Mexican politicians. Former Tamaulipas governor Francisco Cabeza de Vaca published a video in which individuals tied to Mexico’s political elite said El Chapo Isidro had given suitcases full of money to current Tamaulipas Governor Americo Villarreal and to Sinaloa Governor Ruben Rocha Moya. Rocha Moya remains a fugitive from the U.S. Department of Justice, wanted on drug conspiracy and weapons charges, even though Mexico’s government has been refusing to arrest him and extradite him.

sources.text:
FBI’s Most Wanted Cartel Leader Captured
Mexican federal forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as “El Chapo Isidro” or “Chapito Isidro,” on Friday evening in Guasave, Sinaloa. The operation was conducted by special forces of the Mexican Army and the National Guard, in coordination with military personnel assigned to the Sinaloa State Secretariat of Public Security, and relied on intelligence shared with U.S. agencies.
Meza Flores had been identified by U.S. authorities as the leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization, also referred to as the Guasave Cartel or Los Mazatlecos. The group maintained operational ties to the Beltrán Leyva organization, in which he previously served as a high-ranking member and associate of Alfredo Beltrán Leyva.
U.S. records describe the organization as involved in the production, transportation, and distribution of multi-ton quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States over more than two decades.
On February 4, 2025, the FBI added Meza Flores to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list as the 533rd individual placed on the roster. The U.S. Department of State’s Narcotics Rewards Program had offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest or conviction.
He faced federal charges in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia stemming from a May 2012 indictment and a November 2019 superseding indictment. The charges included conspiracy to manufacture and distribute large quantities of methamphetamine, cocaine, heroin, and marijuana for importation into the United States, as well as use and possession of a firearm.
An FBI spokesperson said at the time of the listing that he was “accused of spending the last 20 years flooding the U.S. with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, and other deadly drugs” and that his organization was also accused of kidnapping, extortion, torture, and murder.
Mexican authorities reported that the November 20 operation began after the target’s location was determined through technological means. Special forces approached by multiple land routes using stealth, established security perimeters, and came under attack by gunfire and explosives before entering the residence and taking Meza Flores into custody along with two other senior cartel leaders.
According to Mexico’s National Detention Registry, the capture occurred at approximately 19:50 hours. The three men were transferred by Mexican Air Force aircraft to Mexico City and placed at the disposal of competent authorities. Meza Flores faced a Mexican arrest warrant for organized crime and crimes against health, as well as a U.S. extradition order related to drug distribution conspiracy.
Following the operation, armed groups established roadblocks in municipalities including Ahome, Guamúchil, Guasave, and Navolato. Authorities activated contingency measures to clear routes and protect the population. Gunfire in Guasave prompted the evacuation of spectators from Kuroda Park during a baseball game, and vehicles were burned in the area.
Such activity is common following arrests of high-level cartel leaders.
The joint intelligence effort underscored continued U.S.-Mexico cooperation against major trafficking organizations.
Meza Flores’s placement on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted list reflected the scale of the trafficking attributed to his network.
The multi-ton quantities of fentanyl and other drugs cited in charging documents highlight the organization’s impact on U.S. communities.
Extradition proceedings are expected to follow once Mexican legal processes are completed.
The use of technology to locate the target marked a key element of the successful operation.
Resistance during the raid, including explosives, indicated the level of security surrounding the fugitive.
Post-arrest violence in surrounding areas required additional security responses from Mexican forces.
The capture removes a long-sought figure from active leadership of a major Sinaloa-based trafficking group.

sources.news_title: Mexico Captures FBI Top 10 Fugitive ‘Chapo Isidro’ With U.S. Intelligence
sources.text:
Mexican army and National Guard special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “Chapo Isidro,” in Guasave, Sinaloa, on Friday with help from U.S. intelligence. The FBI Ten Most Wanted fugitive faces federal charges of narcoterrorism and conspiracy to traffic fentanyl and other drugs into the United States, the Justice Department announced Saturday.
A U.S. Homeland Security Task Force that included the FBI and Homeland Security Investigations supported the Mexican operation. The FBI added Meza Flores to its Ten Most Wanted list on February 4, 2025, nearly 13 years after federal prosecutors first charged him.
“This is the 11th Ten Most Wanted fugitive captured under the Trump administration,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in the announcement.
Four Mexican soldiers die in the operation
Four Mexican infantry soldiers died on their way to reinforce troops in Guasave. Seven suspected attackers also died, and Mexican forces arrested eight people in all, Mexico’s Defense Ministry reported. Hospitals across Sinaloa treated about 10 wounded service members, state Health Secretary Cuitláhuac González Galindo told reporters Sunday.
Meza Flores, 44, remained in Mexican custody at the federal organized crime prosecutor’s office in Mexico City on Sunday. He faces a Mexican arrest warrant on organized crime and drug allegations and a separate warrant for extradition to the United States, the ministry said. Neither government had announced a transfer date as of November 22.
Six federal charges
A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., returned a six-count superseding indictment on September 25. Prosecutors allege that under Meza Flores’ leadership, the Sinaloa Cartel shipped tons of drugs into the United States, including fentanyl, methamphetamine, heroin, cocaine and marijuana. Prosecutors say he commanded gunmen who controlled territory around Guasave and Los Mochis. Mexico’s Defense Ministry identified him as the head of the Beltrán Leyva organization and an ally of the Sinaloa Cartel’s Mayos faction.
The other charges include running a continuing criminal enterprise, conspiracies to launder money and provide material support to a terrorist organization, and a firearms offense involving a machine gun and a destructive device.
Meza Flores shares part of his alias with Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán. A federal judge in Brooklyn gave Guzmán, the former Sinaloa Cartel leader, a sentence of life plus 30 years in 2019, as The Dallas Express previously reported.

sources.news_title: Mexican military captures cartel leader after a night of violence
sources.text:
The Mexican military has captured Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, a high-profile cartel leader and one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives. The operation, which took place in the state of Sinaloa on Friday, resulted in intense violence that left at least 11 people dead, including four Mexican soldiers and seven alleged cartel gunmen.
CNN reported that the arrest of the man known as El Chapo Isidro is a major development in the region’s ongoing security efforts. Meza-Flores, who reportedly led the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization, was taken into custody alongside his second-in-command, Germán “N,” and a suspected financial operator named José “N.” Mexican officials confirmed the group was moved to Mexico City following the operation.
The capture triggered violence across the city of Guasave. In a state where baseball is reportedly bigger than soccer, CNN noted that the violence reached the local baseball stadium during a match between the Venados de Mazatlán and the Algodoneros de Guasave. Geolocated footage reportedly shows fans scrambling for cover as gunfire rang out, with a person shouting, “Get down, duck down, down, down!” as the crowd fled the stands.
The violence spread across the city
According to the outlet, the game announcers on the broadcast informed viewers that the game was being suspended due to a security incident. One local told CNN that private hospitals were taken over by armed individuals, while various businesses, including gas stations and convenience stores, were set on fire. According to the Associated Press, firefights broke out around 7:00 PM on Friday, which forced residents to hide in grocery stores and other locations.
Meza Flores is the second cartel leader to be arrested in recent months, and Mexican officials stated that they used stealth and surprise to locate him. However, the operation quickly turned into a prolonged standoff, with a federal official telling the Associated Press that authorities were unable to extract the prisoner until 4:00 AM on Saturday due to at least 10 roadblocks maintained by burning vehicles.
Security forces faced gunfire and explosives throughout the night. CNN reported that footage from the city showed what seemed to be Mexican security forces helicopters circling the city while they fired at the ground. Locals told the outlet that convoys of “heavily armed civilians” roamed the streets “firing shots.”
The US Ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, reportedly said on X that the operation resulted from “strategic intelligence sharing between the United States and Mexico.” He added, “Terrorist Cartels and criminals will be brought to justice. And together we will make both our nations safer.” The DEA also praised the efforts, calling the arrest a significant blow to a violent criminal organization.
Despite the high-profile nature of the arrest, security analysts warn that the strategy of targeting individual leaders could lead to more violence in the long run. According to AP News, David Saucedo, a security expert, noted, “What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don’t dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact.”
Saucedo reportedly called the operation “a product of pressure from the United States.” He claimed that only zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores leaves the remaining organization open to power struggles and violence between rival factions.
As of Saturday, an uneasy calm had returned to Guasave, with burned-out trucks and destroyed stores remaining as evidence of the overnight conflict. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch confirmed that armed forces would stay in the area to maintain order.

MEXICO CITY — A Mexican drug kingpin who was one of the FBI’s 10 most-wanted fugitives was captured in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, the Mexican government said on Saturday, in an operation that unleashed chaos as cartel henchmen and military forces clashed.
The arrest on Friday night of the drug trafficker, Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, who is known as El Chapo Isidro, was a major victory in Mexico’s campaign against its largest criminal organizations. Meza Flores was among the most powerful traffickers in Sinaloa, where a war between rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel has killed thousands and plunged the state into relentless violence.
Mexico’s Defense Ministry said in a statement Saturday that the operation to capture Meza Flores had been carried out in coordination with U.S. agencies. Representatives for the State Department and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
“This operation underscores the critical importance of intelligence sharing in targeting dangerous cartel leaders,” the Drug Enforcement Administration said in a statement. It commended the Mexican authorities who conducted the operation, calling the capture a “significant blow” to the cartel.
Two more cartel operatives were arrested along with Meza Flores: his second-in-command and his financial operator, Mexico’s security minister, Omar García Harfuch, said on social media on Saturday.
President Donald Trump said earlier Friday at the White House that he told Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum at a summit this past week in China that cartels were running her country. Sheinbaum has publicly rejected that characterization.
Meza Flores was the leader of the Beltrán Leyva drug trafficking organization, originally part of the powerful Sinaloa Cartel, before starting his own group, which is known as the Meza-Flores criminal organization, in Sinaloa.
U.S. authorities describe the group as a heavily armed and violent organization that controls drug production and distribution in parts of Mexico. They accuse it of trafficking large quantities of fentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine and marijuana into the United States.
Meza Flores shares a similar nickname but is not related to Joaquín Guzmán Loera, the imprisoned Mexican drug kingpin known as El Chapo who helped run the Sinaloa Cartel before his arrest in 2014. The two men became rivals in Mexico’s drug trade and fought a bloody turf war in the late 2000s.
Meza Flores has never been as prominent as his namesake. But even though he operated mostly below the radar, he has a reputation as a major — and violent — player in the Mexican drug trade. He was the “dominant crime boss” in northern Sinaloa, according to Adrián López, publisher of a leading newspaper in the state capital that has closely covered the cartel wars for decades.
The operation to capture Meza Flores threw the northern city of Guasave into turmoil on Friday night as federal forces were attacked, according to a post on social platform X by the state’s public security agency, which urged residents to shelter in place and avoid a major highway connecting the northern and southern parts of the state.
Trucks burned across major roads and gunfire rang out in several neighborhoods, local news outlets reported. In footage shared by Mexican TV networks, helicopters flew overhead, one appearing to fire toward the ground.
A professional baseball game was suspended as gunfire rang out. Videos posted on social media showed fans streaming into the stadium’s corridors for shelter and players running off the field. In another recording shared by a Mexican TV network, a reporter covering the clashes ducked between two cars as shooting broke out. As the firefight ensued, some people took refuge in supermarkets, businesses, cinemas and churches.
By Saturday morning, the aftermath of the violence was evident across Guasave. Incinerated cars slumped along the roads; military troops guarded the nearby Los Mochis international airport, where several flights were canceled; and gas stations stood charred.
Federal prosecutors in Washington, who filed indictments against Meza Flores in 2012 and 2019, updated the charges only two months ago, suggesting that U.S. authorities were continuing their pursuit of him. At that time, the prosecutors asked a judge overseeing the case to cancel an arrest warrant issued in Meza Flores’ name in 2019 because authorities planned to seek his arrest on the updated third indictment.
That indictment built on the ones before it but added a few new counts, including terrorism charges accusing Meza Flores of acting in support of the Sinaloa Cartel. One month after Trump returned to the White House, the State Department designated the cartel as a foreign terrorism organization. The agency had offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to Meza Flores’ arrest or conviction.
The new indictment also accused Meza Flores of abducting a member of the Mexican national guard in Oaxaca in October 2022 and killing him. It charged him further with smuggling about 6,000 kilograms, or more than 6 tons, of methamphetamine across the border near Eagle Pass, Texas, in February 2024.
Meza Flores’ group, previously a bitter rival of the Sinaloa Cartel, recently allied with a faction of the cartel called Los Mayos, according to López. Los Mayos has been fighting another faction called Los Chapitos for control of the cartel since 2024, after one of its founders, Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, was taken into U.S. custody.
Trump has vowed to “dismantle” the cartels and frequently raised the prospect of sending U.S. military forces into Mexico. “We can’t let the cartels run Mexico,” he said at a news conference Friday, after confirming that he had told Sheinbaum that he thought that it was the case that drug organizations were too powerful in Mexico. “They’re our neighbor.”
Sheinbaum has repeatedly ruled out U.S. military intervention on Mexican soil, even as her government has deepened security cooperation with Washington.
Under pressure from Trump, Sheinbaum’s government has intensified its nationwide crackdown on criminal groups. Mexican authorities have arrested tens of thousands of people, seized hundreds of tons of drugs and destroyed thousands of clandestine labs and other sites used to make drugs. Mexico has also transferred dozens of drug trafficking suspects into U.S. custody.

As the firefight ensued, some people took refuge in supermarkets, businesses, cinemas and churches.

Federal prosecutors in Washington, who filed indictments against Meza Flores in 2012 and 2019, updated the charges only two months ago, suggesting that US authorities were continuing their pursuit of him. At that time, the prosecutors asked a judge overseeing the case to cancel an arrest warrant issued in Meza Flores’ name in 2019 because authorities planned to seek his arrest on the updated third indictment.
That indictment built on the ones before it but added a few new counts, including terrorism charges accusing Meza Flores of acting in support of the Sinaloa Cartel. One month after Trump returned to the White House, the State Department designated the cartel as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The agency had offered a reward of up to $US5 million ($7.5 million) for information leading to Meza Flores’ arrest or conviction.
The new indictment also accused Meza Flores of abducting a member of the Mexican national guard in Oaxaca in October 2022 and killing him. It charged him further with smuggling about 6000 kilograms of methamphetamine across the border near Eagle Pass, Texas, in February 2024.
Meza Flores’ group, previously a bitter rival of the Sinaloa Cartel, recently allied with a faction of the cartel called Los Mayos, according to López. Los Mayos has been fighting another faction called Los Chapitos for control of the cartel since 2024, after one of its founders, Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, was taken into US custody.

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro” and one of the FBI's top 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured by Mexican authorities overnight from Friday into Saturday, with intelligence assistance from the Trump administration, according to Mexico's Secretary of Security and Citizen Protection, Omar Garcia Harfuch.
The 44-year-old international drug lord had a $5 million reward offered for information leading to his arrest. His detention immediately triggered a burst of violence in Mexico's Sinaloa state, leaving at least 11 people dead, according to authorities.
An overnight firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen left residents of the city of Guasave terrorised, with trucks and businesses set ablaze.
Mexico's Defence Cabinet confirmed on Saturday afternoon that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed in the clashes.
According to US and Mexican authorities, Meza Flores rose from humble beginnings as a scrap metal dealer and small-time drug trafficker to become one of the most powerful figures in the Mexican drug trade.
His history of trafficking stretches back more than 20 years, during which the FBI says he spent years smuggling heroin, cocaine, fentanyl, and other drugs into the United States.
Despite his notoriety, capturing Meza Flores proved difficult for both countries.
Also known as "Chapito Isidro," he is of relatively small stature—standing 5 feet 6 inches tall and weighing about 160 pounds—and maintained a notoriously low profile while his organisation controlled key drug-transportation routes and manufacturing laboratories.
Meza Flores first rose to prominence leading the violent Beltrán Leyva drug trafficking organisation, which the US Treasury Department said split from the Sinaloa Cartel in 2008, sparking a bloody regional power struggle similar to the cartel infighting seen in Sinaloa in recent years.
He later led his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organisation (TCO)—also known as Los Mazatlecos—for over two decades. Beyond drug trafficking, the FBI and Mexico's government have accused the group of kidnapping, extortion, torture, and murder.
The US State Department has also linked the group to numerous deaths of Mexican police, military forces, and rival criminals, noting it is part of a network of warring criminal groups terrorising civilians across Mexico.
"The Meza-Flores TCO has been responsible for smuggling multi-ton quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, and marijuana into the United States," the State Department said in a 2025 statement announcing a reward for his arrest.
Meza Flores is also allied with "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel currently warring for control of the Mexican state. The Sinaloa Cartel was designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the Trump administration last year.
Meza Flores's capture comes more than 14 years after he was first indicted by the United States. Seven years after that initial indictment, a federal superseding indictment and arrest warrant were issued for him in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, charging him with multiple drug-trafficking violations as well as the use and possession of a firearm, according to the FBI.

sources.text:
Mexico detains top cartel boss ‘El Chapo Isidro’, setting off a burst of violence in Sinaloa
Loading article...
MEXICO CITY (AP)
Gunfire rang out, trucks burned and Mexican forces clashed with cartel gunmen in the state of Sinaloa overnight as Mexican authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’.
Meza Flores was one of the Federal Bureau of Investigations’ (FBI) 10 most wanted fugitives and a top cartel leader from the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation wanted for trafficking drugs to the United States (US) and illegally carrying firearms.
Mexico’s government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the US coordinated to detain Meza Flores.
He was also a key ally to ‘Los Mayos’, a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.
Authorities in the US and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. US President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico’s government to go after criminal groups.
However experts warn that it could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.
Mexican forces’ move against cartel fuels violence
Mexican authorities said they used “stealth and surprise” to capture Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. He was later taken by aircraft to Mexico City to appear before prosecutors.
Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage escorting a man through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck. No casualties have been reported so far as a result of the operation.
The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence overnight with calm setting in Saturday morning.
Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.
As a result, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn’t authorized to discuss the case.
“Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary,” the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least “10 roadblocks” with burning vehicles on Guasave’s streets.
Terror in Sinaloa
Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.
“Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks,” Sánchez told The Associated Press.
She said the city’s firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.
“Everything looks calm today,” Sánchez said.
Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians.
Capture prompts celebration and warnings
Meza Flores’ detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.
The US and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities.
“The capture of El Chapo Isidro delivers a significant blow to a ruthless criminal organization that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities,” the DEA said in a statement. “This operation underscores the critical importance of intelligence sharing in targeting dangerous cartel leaders.”
García Harfuch called the detention “an important step in pacifying Sinaloa.”
Sheinbaum’s government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as ‘El Mencho’, who was killed by the military in February.
Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the US increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy, which critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.
The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.
“What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States,” Saucedo said. “What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don’t dismantle the entire organisation. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact.”

sources.news_title: Mexico captures FBI most-wanted kingpin ‘Chapo Isidro’ in Sinaloa raid that leaves 11 dead

MEXICO CITY, Nov 22 — Mexico’s military announced yesterday that it had captured a drug kingpin on the FBI’s list of 10 most wanted fugitives in an operation that left four soldiers and seven suspected gunmen dead.
Fausto Isidro Meza, alias “Chapo Isidro,” was captured Friday night during a special forces raid in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, along with his alleged second-in-command and a financial operator for his criminal organization.
The Mexican defense ministry said seven suspected attackers were killed and eight people arrested during the operation, including the three senior gang figures.
Four soldiers sent to reinforce security in the town of Guasave were also killed as gang members mounted fierce resistance to their leader’s arrest, it said.
The military seized a .50-caliber rifle, a grenade launcher, grenades, other firearms, drugs and cash. It said there were no reports of civilian casualties.
The operation sparked panic across the surrounding area, with gunfire forcing the suspension of a professional baseball game in Guasave, local media reported.
Unverified videos posted on social media showed people running inside the stadium amid shouts of “Get down, get down!” as bursts of gunfire rang out nearby.
Another video appeared to show a hovering military helicopter firing a machine gun.
Violence also erupted in other parts of Sinaloa, where suspected gang members erected improvised roadblocks.
An unverified video circulating on social media overnight appeared to show a detained Chapo Isidro urging his associates to stand down, warning that “children, women, innocent people” could be put in harm’s way.
The violence echoed the aftermath of a military operation in February that killed Nemesio Oseguera, alias “El Mencho,” leader of the powerful Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG).
His supporters retaliated by setting fire to businesses and blocking roads across 20 of Mexico’s 32 states.
US intelligence ‘coordination’
Chapo Isidro, 44, leads a drug trafficking organization affiliated with the Beltran Leyva gang and allied with one of two rival factions of the powerful Sinaloa cartel, according to US and Mexican authorities.
He faces criminal charges in both Mexico and the United States.
The FBI had placed him on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives, while the US State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest.
Giving his name as Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, the FBI bulletin said his group is responsible for importing “large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States.”
The US Drug Enforcement Administration welcomed his capture as “a significant victory against one of Mexico’s most violent criminal networks.”
The agency said the organization had fueled violence in Mexico for decades while trafficking drugs, including fentanyl, into the United States, and commended Mexican authorities for the operation.
In July, Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, a longtime leader of the Sinaloa cartel, was sentenced to life in prison in New York.
Zambada was a former associate of notorious drug trafficker Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman, who was extradited to the United States in 2017 and is also serving a life sentence.
Chapo Isidro’s capture comes just days after Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum met US counterpart Donald Trump on the sidelines of a summit in Asia.
Trump, who has pushed Mexico to do more to tackle drug gangs, said Friday that the two had discussed trade and security.
”We’re working with her on the cartels because the cartels are running Mexico. I told her that, and we can’t let the cartels run Mexico. They’re our neighbor,” he told reporters at the White House.
The Mexican military said the operation was conducted “following coordination” with US intelligence in the “framework of bilateral cooperation.”
Earlier this year, Sheinbaum faced political pressure over revelations that US intelligence personnel were operating in Mexico without her government’s approval following the deaths of two reportedly CIA agents in a road accident. — AFP

Four Soldiers Die in Mexico Cartel Boss Raid
The arrest of one of the FBI’s most wanted men cost the Mexican army four lives in a single night. Prosecutors have yet to say what charges the detained leader faces.
Security: Mexico
Four Mexican soldiers died on Friday night while rushing to back up a raid in Guasave, a city in Sinaloa state on Mexico’s Pacific coast. Seven suspected gunmen also died, the Defence Ministry, known as Defensa, said on Saturday 21 November 2026.
The raid ended with the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias “Chapo Isidro”, a cartel leader on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted list. Our first report covered the capture; the ministry’s new count shows what it cost.
Key Facts
- Who. Four soldiers and seven suspected gunmen died; eight people were detained, among them cartel boss Meza Flores.
- What. The soldiers were driving to reinforce the Guasave raid when armed men tried to block the arrest.
- When. Friday 20 November 2026 into Saturday 21 November; Defensa gave the toll on Saturday.
- Power Index. Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 70.8 points (November 2026 edition).
- As of. 21 November 2026, 7 p.m. Eastern Time (ET).
The arrest of one of the FBI’s most wanted men cost the Mexican army four lives in a single night. Prosecutors have yet to say what charges the detained leader faces.
What Defensa Says Happened
Defensa said on X, the social network, that the four soldiers were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave when members of the organisation met them with armed resistance. The ministry sent condolences to the families and promised them institutional support.
Seven suspected attackers died and eight people were detained, Defensa said. Five of the detainees, among them Pánfilo “N” (Mexican officials withhold surnames of suspects not yet tried), a first cousin of Meza Flores described as the group’s logistics operator, were handed to the Attorney General’s Office (FGR) in Culiacán, the state capital.
Meza Flores and his two aides, Germán “N” and José “N”, landed in Mexico City at 5:20 a.m. on Saturday (6:20 a.m. Eastern Time, ET) aboard a military transport plane. They went to FEMDO, the federal prosecutors’ unit that handles organised crime, which will decide their legal position.
Troops seized a Barrett .50-calibre rifle, a heavy sniper weapon, ten other firearms, a grenade launcher and two hand grenades. Defensa said that so far it had no report of bystanders harmed.
Eleven Dead in One Night
Eleven deaths in one operation is a heavy toll even for Sinaloa. Large federal forces remain deployed there.
The nearest local comparison is La Brecha, a rural community in Guasave, where a clash on Monday 3 November 2025 left 13 suspected gunmen dead, as we reported at the time. Friday’s toll of 11, four of them soldiers, is of the same order.
The group’s members tried to block the capture, Defensa said, and the four soldiers were killed in that clash. The ministry said it will keep working against organised crime in Sinaloa.
Why Washington Is Watching
The FBI added Meza Flores to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list on 4 February 2025. The US State Department offered up to US$5 million for information leading to his arrest, and the US Treasury’s sanctions office froze his assets in January 2013 under US drug sanctions.
Defensa said the operation followed intelligence coordination with US agencies. It described Meza Flores as head of the Beltrán Leyva organisation, a long-running Mexican trafficking network, and an ally of the Mayos, a faction of the Sinaloa cartel.
The capture took out three roles at once: the alleged leader, his second-in-command and his financial operator, according to Defensa. Whether that weakens the group or sparks a fight over who leads it is not yet known.
What Is Not Known
Neither Defensa nor federal prosecutors have published charges, a court date or an extradition request.

sources.news_title: Capture of cartel leader in Mexico sparks deadly violence in Sinaloa
sources.text:
Capture of cartel leader in Mexico sparks deadly violence in Sinaloa
GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — Heavy gunfire, helicopters and burning trucks marked Mexico’s Sinaloa state Saturday after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” in an operation that left at least 11 people dead.
Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after the firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized.
Mexico’s Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed.
The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.
Mexico’s government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.
He was also a key ally to “Los Mayos,” a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.
Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico’s government to go after criminal groups.
As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.
Mexican forces’ move against cartel fuels violence
The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city.
Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.
“The fighting was happening all over Guasave,” said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. “It spread throughout the city.”
Mexican authorities said that they used “stealth and surprise” to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him.
Video shared by Mexico’s Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities.
Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn’t authorized to discuss the case.
“Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary,” the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least “10 roadblocks” with burning vehicles on Guasave’s streets.
Terror in Sinaloa
Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.
“Last night, many businesses were burned … along with cars and trucks,” Sánchez told The Associated Press.
She said that the city’s firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.
An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. He lamented the deaths of the four soldiers killed in the operation.
Burned-out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday.
“The aftermath of last night’s war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down,” Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico.
Guasave residents remained “very afraid” because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said.
Capture prompts celebration and warnings
Meza Flores’ detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.
The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities.
“Results like these don’t happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together,” U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. “We will continue the hunt.”
Mexican Security Secretary García Harfuch called the detention “an important step in pacifying Sinaloa.”
Sheinbaum’s government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as “ El Mencho,” who was killed by the military in February.
Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.
The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.
“What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States,” Saucedo said. “What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don’t dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact.”
___
Janetsky and Sánchez reported from Mexico City. Associated Press writer Thomas Strong contributed to this report from Washington.

Mexico Captures 'El Chapo Isidro' in Sinaloa Raid
sources.text:
Mexican special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, the cartel boss known as “El Chapo Isidro” and one of the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives, in Guasave, Sinaloa, on the night of Friday, November 20. Mexico’s Defense Ministry said the operation followed intelligence coordination with U.S. agencies. The fighting that followed left at least 11 people dead, including four Mexican soldiers, according to the Associated Press.
What Mexico’s government says happened
In its statement, Mexico’s Secretariat of National Defense (Sedena) said the arrest came from “coordination between intelligence agencies” of Sedena and the United States “within the framework of bilateral cooperation.” National Guard special forces known as “Lobos” and Army special forces known as “Murciélagos” carried out the raid, alongside Army special forces assigned to Sinaloa’s state security ministry, according to the statement as published by El Financiero.
Sedena described Meza Flores as head of the “Beltrán Leyva” criminal organization, allied with the “Mayos” faction of the Sinaloa (Pacific) Cartel. Two other men were detained with him: Germán “N,” alias “Serafín,” named as the group’s second in command, and José “N,” described as its financial operator. The AP reported that authorities detained eight people in total.
Troops came under gunfire and explosives as they closed in, Mexican officials said. Vehicles and businesses burned and roadblocks went up across the municipality of about 290,000 people, the AP reported. Because of the violence, forces could not fly Meza Flores out of Guasave until 4 a.m. Saturday, a federal official told the AP on condition of anonymity, describing cartel members holding at least “10 roadblocks.” “Getting him out was extraordinary,” the official said. A Mexican Pacific League baseball game between the Venados de Mazatlán and the Algodoneros was suspended as gunfire broke out, El Financiero reported.
The Defense Ministry said seven alleged cartel gunmen and four soldiers were killed. Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch lamented the deaths of the four soldiers and called the arrest “an important step” toward peace in Sinaloa. Meza Flores was flown to Mexico City to be handed to prosecutors.
What the U.S. case says
According to the FBI’s wanted page, Meza Flores, born June 19, 1982, was first indicted on May 2, 2012, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. A superseding indictment and arrest warrant followed on November 26, 2019. The charges are conspiracy to manufacture and distribute methamphetamine and to distribute cocaine, heroin and marijuana for import into the United States, plus use and possession of a firearm. The FBI added him to the Ten Most Wanted list on February 4, 2025. The State Department’s Narcotics Rewards Program offered up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest or conviction.
The FBI calls him the “alleged leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization,” a “heavily armed, major drug-trafficking organization” it says moves heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States. Sedena said he faces a Mexican arrest warrant for organized crime and drug offenses and a U.S. extradition warrant for conspiracy to distribute drugs.
Washington praised the arrest. “Results like these don’t happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust,” U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson wrote on X. “We will continue the hunt.” The Drug Enforcement Administration also commended Mexican authorities, the AP reported.
What is unclear or disputed
The U.S. role. Mexico credited U.S. intelligence but gave few details of how the two governments worked together, the AP reported. The White House, State Department and FBI did not immediately respond to Reuters.
Which organization he ran. The labels differ. Sedena calls him head of the Beltrán Leyva organization. Reuters described him as “one of the leaders” of the Beltrán Leyva cartel. The FBI names his own Meza-Flores organization. The AP reported he rose to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later formed his own group.
Earlier near-misses. This is not the first big operation against him in Guasave. In November 2025, after a clash between federal forces and gunmen there, Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya said Meza Flores was not among those detained, Plano Informativo reported at the time.
Whether it will reduce violence. Mexican security analyst David Saucedo told the AP that the arrest marks another return to the “kingpin strategy,” which experts say often sets off violent power struggles. Sinaloa is already split by a war between Sinaloa Cartel factions, and Meza Flores was a key ally of the “Mayos” side.
Analysis: pressure from Washington
The following is Right Side News analysis, not reported fact. Reuters noted the arrest comes as Mexico has captured or killed a string of high-profile suspected traffickers under pressure from Washington, while President Trump has repeatedly threatened unilateral military action against cartels inside Mexico. President Claudia Sheinbaum’s government killed Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, “El Mencho,” in February, the AP reported. The Trump administration designated the Sinaloa Cartel a foreign terrorist organization last year. Whether Mexico extradites Meza Flores quickly, as Washington will want, is the next test. No extradition date has been announced, and any timeline is speculation at this point.

After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. Meza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. The Public Security Secretariat of Sinaloa reported an attack on federal personnel in Guasave on Friday, November 20, 2026, and warned the public to stay indoors.
“The SSPSinaloa reports that, this Friday, November 20, 2026, an attack on federal personnel occurred in the municipality of Guasave. The public is asked to stay safe indoors and avoid the area, as well as to refrain from traveling on roads,”
Video shared by TV Azteca showed low-flying Mexican military helicopters firing during the clash in what appeared to be a residential area. The Associated Press reported blockades built with trucks set alight that tied up multiple highways into the city of roughly 300,000 people.
Interim Governor Graciela Domínguez Nava said residents became stranded along parts of highways in Sinaloa as the violence escalated.
At Kuroda Park, a Mexican Pacific League game between the Algodoneros de Guasave and the Venados de Mazatlán was underway when gunshots were heard. Players called time and sprinted for the dugouts. Broadcast commentators told viewers the situation had changed fast.
“There is an off-field situation,”
Another call followed:
“There is a national security situation and we’d better pause and we’ll be reporting any developments in the game,”
League officials later canceled the rest of the contest and said none of the fighting took place inside the stadium.
“In light of security-related incidents that have occurred over the last few hours in the city of Guasave, the Liga Mexicana del Pacífico Banamex, in coordination with local authorities and with the goal of safeguarding the well-being of our fans, has decided to cancel the game between the Venados de Mazatlán and the Algodoneros de Guasave at Kuroda Park,”
The FBI described the Meza-Flores organization as “heavily armed and violent,” saying the group used “gun battles, kidnapping, murder, torture, and extortion to maintain control of their territory.” U.S. officials have also tied the group to the killing of multiple law enforcement officers and rival cartel members in Sinaloa.
For American communities living with the downstream costs of cartel supply lines, the arrest removes a high-value target who sat on the FBI’s most-wanted board for years. The case still has to move through Mexican custody, transfer, and extradition. The street-level chaos that followed the raid shows how these groups still answer capture with open force.
Casualty figures from the gunfight were not released in the initial reports. What is clear is the sequence: a joint U.S.-Mexico strike, three senior figures in custody, military helicopters in the fight, civilians ordered indoors, and a professional baseball game shut down for public safety.
Cartels do not surrender quietly when their bosses fall. Taxpayers and border communities pay the price for every year those bosses stay free, and they deserve operations that keep ending that way.

sources.news_title: Mexico Captures FBI’s Most-Wanted Cartel Leader ‘El Chapo Isidro’ as Deadly Violence Erupts in Sinaloa
sources.text:
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
MEXICO CITY — Mexican military forces have captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, the alleged drug cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro” who appeared on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, following a major operation in Sinaloa that triggered deadly clashes between security forces and suspected cartel gunmen.
The arrest took place Friday night, Nov. 20, in Guasave, Sinaloa, and was announced Saturday by Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch. Authorities also detained two senior members of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organization, including its second-in-command and a financial operator.
According to Reuters reporting on the operation, Mexican army and National Guard special forces carried out the arrests with intelligence assistance from the United States.
The operation sparked extensive violence across Guasave as suspected cartel members confronted military personnel, blocked highways with burning vehicles and attacked security forces attempting to remove the detained suspects.
Mexican authorities reported Saturday that at least 11 people were killed, including seven suspected cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers, according to The Associated Press.
Meza Flores, 44, had been sought by American authorities for years over allegations that he directed a major drug-trafficking organization responsible for transporting heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States.
The FBI’s wanted notice identifies him as the alleged leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization, a heavily armed trafficking network based in Sinaloa.
The U.S. State Department had offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading directly to his arrest or conviction.
Mexican defense officials said the operation resulted from coordination between military intelligence agencies in Mexico and the United States.
Special forces established a security perimeter around a building where Meza Flores was believed to be staying. When suspected cartel members attacked with firearms and explosives, troops entered the residence and arrested him.
The two other detainees were identified by Mexican authorities as Germán N., known as “Serafín,” the organization’s second-in-command, and José N., described as a financial operator.
Mexican authorities commonly withhold suspects’ full surnames in official announcements under domestic legal procedures.
The arrests triggered an armed response that spread through parts of Guasave, a municipality of approximately 290,000 residents.
Videos circulating online showed military helicopters operating over the city, vehicles burning along highways and civilians fleeing gunfire during a baseball game.
Residents also reported businesses and gas stations being set ablaze as armed groups attempted to obstruct military movements.
The fighting began around 7 p.m. Friday and continued into the early morning hours of Saturday.
Security forces encountered at least 10 roadblocks involving burning vehicles, complicating efforts to transport the detainees out of the area.
A federal official familiar with the operation told the Associated Press that Mexican forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until approximately 4 a.m. Saturday because of the intensity of the armed resistance.
Authorities subsequently transported him to Mexico City to appear before federal prosecutors.
The Mexican government said additional troops would remain deployed in Sinaloa to protect residents and restore security.
García Harfuch described the arrests as an important development in the government’s campaign against organized crime.
“These detentions are an important step in pacifying Sinaloa,” he said.
Residents described widespread fear as gunfire erupted near populated areas and people sought shelter in stores and other buildings.
Firefighters were reportedly unable to respond immediately to burning vehicles and businesses because of the ongoing violence.
By Saturday morning, burned-out trucks remained along roads leading into Guasave, while security personnel continued clearing barricades and monitoring the area.
The capture represents a significant setback for the Beltrán Leyva organization, which has operated for decades as part of Mexico’s drug-trafficking networks.
Meza Flores rose through the organization’s ranks before establishing his own trafficking operation, which maintained influence across portions of Sinaloa and other areas of Mexico.
He was also considered an important ally of Los Mayos, a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel involved in a prolonged conflict with rival criminal groups.
That alliance made his organization part of a broader struggle for control of trafficking routes, territory and criminal operations in northwestern Mexico.
According to CBS News’ coverage of the arrest, the operation occurred amid continuing violence involving rival cartel factions in the state.
Federal prosecutors in the United States first indicted Meza Flores in May 2012 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.
A superseding indictment and federal arrest warrant followed in November 2019, alleging drug-trafficking offenses and violations involving firearms.
American authorities accused him of participating in a conspiracy to manufacture and distribute substantial quantities of illegal drugs for importation into the United States.
The charges included allegations involving at least 500 grams of methamphetamine, five kilograms of cocaine, one kilogram of heroin and 1,000 kilograms of marijuana.
The FBI also identified fentanyl among the substances allegedly distributed by his organization.
Meza Flores was added to the bureau’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in February 2025.
Mexican authorities have also sought him on organized crime and drug-related charges, while the United States has requested his extradition.
It was not immediately clear Saturday when formal extradition proceedings would begin or whether he would first face prosecution in Mexico.
The arrest comes as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces sustained pressure from President Donald Trump to intensify operations against drug cartels and disrupt narcotics trafficking into the United States.
Trump has repeatedly demanded stronger action against criminal organizations and threatened unilateral military operations inside Mexico if authorities fail to curb cartel activity.
Sheinbaum’s administration has expanded security operations targeting senior cartel leaders, while emphasizing that cooperation with the United States must respect Mexican sovereignty.
Earlier this year, Mexican forces killed Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as “El Mencho,” the leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, during a military operation that also triggered violent retaliation.
The arrest of Meza Flores adds to a series of operations targeting prominent organized crime figures.
U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson welcomed the latest capture and emphasized the importance of bilateral intelligence cooperation.
“Results like these don’t happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together,” Johnson said.
“We will continue the hunt.”
Mexican security officials also credited cooperation between the countries’ intelligence agencies for identifying Meza Flores’ location and supporting the operation.
Despite the arrests, security analysts warned that removing cartel leaders does not necessarily dismantle the organizations operating beneath them.
Drug-trafficking groups frequently maintain regional commanders, financial networks and armed enforcement units capable of continuing operations after senior figures are detained.
In Sinaloa, where rival factions have fought for control of territory, the removal of a major criminal leader could also create additional competition among remaining organizations.
Mexican security analyst David Saucedo told the Associated Press that targeting cartel leadership can produce immediate security gains while leaving much of the underlying criminal infrastructure intact.
